source: Del et al. (2026) How Uncertainty Estimation Scales with Sampling in Reasoning Models
finding: Three reasoning models, 17 tasks. Verbalised confidence (VC) beats self-consistency (SC) at low sample counts. Combining the two with just 2 samples beats either alone scaled to 8 samples. The gain is biggest in maths.
numbers: AUROC, maths: VC 71.3 at K=1, 81.4 at K=8 (+10.1). SC at K=2: 70.5 maths, 66.6 STEM, 63.3 humanities. Hybrid SCVC at K=2: 84.2 maths (+12.9 over VC K=1), +6.4 in STEM (73.8 to 80.2) and humanities (68.5 to 74.9). VC and SC at K=8 in maths: 81.4 and 79.6. Further SCVC gain K=2 to 5: +2.7, K=5 to 8: +1.5. Matched-token test, gpt-oss-20b: SC weaker under extended thinking than under shallow thinking, never overtakes VC up to K=8.
quote: avoid single-sample estimation, avoid pure self-consistency
limits: Models are probably gpt-oss-20b, Qwen3-30B-A3B and a DeepSeek-R1 distil (inferred from text and links). AUROC is on final-answer correctness, not on step location. Compares signals at equal sample count; token cost is shown in a figure only. Gains smaller outside maths.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 2 in part. For a reasoning model, plan the monitor as verbalised confidence plus a second sample's agreement. Avoid single-sample estimates and avoid agreement alone. Re-test on our own tasks, since non-maths gains saturate after K=2.

source: Meyer et al. (2026) An Analysis of Training-Free Self-Reported Confidence in Language Models
finding: Small workshop study on 100 TriviaQA questions, two models. Confidence verbalised with the answer separated right from wrong answers very well. Three-sample agreement was much weaker. Agreement repeated shared mistakes. Rewording the confidence prompt moved the scores.
numbers: After audit, 99 questions per model. AUROC verbalised .956 (DeepSeek Flash) and .937 (Claude Sonnet 5); P(True) .920 and .959; 3-sample support .765 and .790; fixed average .973 and .926. Paired bootstrap CIs for the averaged signal all cross zero (e.g. DeepSeek AUROC [-.0289, .0857]). Unanimous support for 4 of 9 DeepSeek errors and 2 of 8 Sonnet errors. Equivalent re-prompts changed scores by .043 to .084 on average and flipped 4.0 to 9.1% of decisions at the .8 threshold. Reworded prompt raised DeepSeek AUROC .920 to .944 but lowered Sonnet .959 to .927 and .909. Uncorrected accuracy .86/.88 versus audited .909/.919.
quote: Re-eliciting confidence for the same fixed answers with equivalent prompts changes scores by 0.043 to 0.084
limits: Only 8 to 9 errors per model, so no powered equivalence test. Easy factual questions (accuracy about .91). One 100-claim biography audit; 15 of 20 automatic contradiction labels were wrong and corrected by hand. Not a reasoning task. Unreviewed workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Cuts against optimism for sample agreement on facts, and for a hard-coded average. Pick the monitor per model, hold the prompt fixed, and audit labels. A fixed confidence prompt wording is part of the instrument (gap 6, in part).

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: A stopping rule for self-consistency: stop drawing samples once the vote lead is statistically safe. Large sample savings with almost no accuracy loss.
numbers: 17 datasets (maths, commonsense, symbolic, code). Up to 7.9x fewer samples, average accuracy drop under 0.1%; average 3.3x fewer on maths with 0.1% drop, 2.9x on commonsense with 0.2% drop. Max 40 generations, temperature 0.7. At fixed sampling cost it beat plain self-consistency by up to 5 points.
limits: The stopping signal is answer agreement, a cheap monitor, not a rate-of-progress or expected-value rule. Majority-vote tasks only. 2023 models. Shared misconceptions (d02) can trigger a confident early stop.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 5. An LLM stop rule exists and works on agreement. It is a stop-on-confidence rule, not Region of Proximal Learning or Callaway-style expected-value stopping, which stay untested.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when a whole window agrees. Cuts the number of samples a lot with similar accuracy. A control scheme picks the cost-quality balance.
numbers: Average samples cut by MATH 33.8%, GSM8K 80.1%, StrategyQA 76.8%, CommonsenseQA 78.5%, Coin Flip 84.2%, Last Letters 67.4%, with comparable accuracy.
limits: Agreement-based stop only. Agrees with d03. Both aim at equal accuracy, not at a payoff.
agent_relevance: Second LLM test of a stopping rule (gap 5). Cheap to add in code: window the retries and stop on agreement.

source: Damani et al. (2024) Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
finding: Predict how much extra compute an input will profit from before spending it, and allocate by that prediction. This is a code-side gate on a prior difficulty monitor (a learned FOK).
numbers: Cuts compute up to 50% at no quality loss, or raises quality up to 10% at fixed compute, across programming, maths and dialog.
quote: reduce computation by up to 50% at no cost to response quality, or improve quality by up to 10%
limits: The difficulty predictor is a trained model, not the LLM's own verbalised FOK. Adaptive best-of-k and routing only, not Self-Refine.
agent_relevance: Gives an equal-compute framework for gap 1: compare gated allocation versus uniform best-of-N at the same total budget. Suggests the gain comes from moving compute to solvable-but-hard items, which fits Cao's low and medium JOL buckets.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Allocating test-time compute by estimated question difficulty beats uniform best-of-N. Sequential revisions versus parallel sampling: the best mix depends on difficulty. For some problems a small model with extra compute beats a 14x larger one.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation matched or beat best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute (revision and PRM-search settings, PaLM 2-S*). Test-time compute can outperform a 14x larger model when the base model has non-trivial success rates.
quote: can improve the efficiency of test-time compute scaling by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline
limits: Difficulty is estimated from sampling or a verifier, not from the model's own confidence. Needs a trained revision model and a PRM. Easy questions favour sequential revisions, hard ones favour parallel search (from the paper's framing).
agent_relevance: Best equal-compute evidence for gap 1: gating by difficulty beats uniform best-of-N. It does not test verbalised FOK/JOL, and it says the right control (revise or resample) depends on the bucket.

source: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang (2025) Why Language Models Hallucinate
finding: Argues that benchmarks that score 'I don't know' as zero push models to guess. Proposes explicit confidence targets in the prompt: answer only above confidence t, wrong answers cost t/(1-t) points. This is the Koriat-Goldsmith payoff setup written for LLMs.
numbers: Examples given: t=0.5 penalty 1, t=0.75 penalty 2, t=0.9 penalty 9; t=0 is plain binary grading. Claims one behaviour is optimal at every t ('behavioral calibration'), auditable by comparing accuracy and error rates across t.
quote: Answer only if you are > t confident, since mistakes are penalized t/(1 - t) points
limits: Theory and position paper. I found no accuracy-quantity curve measured under this scheme in the text I searched. Does not test whether prompting with t makes a model abstain correctly.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open as an experiment but we now have a ready design: run each task at t = 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, report accuracy-quantity curves, and check that abstention rises with t. Code can also apply the threshold to a monitor score instead of asking the model.

source: Kirichenko et al. (2025) AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
finding: 20 datasets, 20 frontier LLMs. Abstention is unsolved and scaling helps little. Reasoning fine-tuning makes abstention worse, including in maths and science. A system prompt helps but does not fix it.
numbers: Reasoning fine-tuned models (DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B and s1) show an average 24% drop in abstention versus their non-reasoning counterparts; reasoning models often hallucinate missing context.
limits: Tests unanswerable and underspecified questions, which differs from abstaining when unlikely to be right. Abstention scored by an LLM judge (Llama 3.1 8B). No payoff manipulation.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a reasoning model cannot be trusted to abstain on its own. Put the abstain decision in code on a monitor score, not in the model. The direction differs from Cacioli's R1 over-withdrawal, so the blanket policy varies by task and probe.

source: Mei et al. (2025) Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
finding: Reasoning models are overconfident, and more so with deeper reasoning. Asking the model to re-read its own trace (introspective UQ) helps some models and hurts others.
numbers: Self-verbalised confidence often above 85%, especially on wrong answers. More overconfident with deeper reasoning. Introspection improved calibration for o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1 but made Claude 3.7 Sonnet worse.
quote: (iii) can become better calibrated through introspection (e.g., o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1) but not uniformly
limits: Calibration (ECE) focus. Model-specific result. I read the abstract and first page only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 (partial analogue): re-reading the model's own trace is a re-read monitor, and it did not help every model. A delayed-JOL style re-read must be tested per model, not assumed.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) Thinking Out Loud: Do Reasoning Models Know When They're Right?
finding: Reasoning distillation and RL improve verbalised calibration step by step, but open reasoning models answer 'I don't know' less often on factuality tests, which suggests weaker awareness of their knowledge limits.
numbers: Open-source reasoning models give significantly fewer 'I don't know' responses than instruction-tuned models (abstract and introduction; exact rates not extracted).
limits: Only the abstract and introduction read. Same direction as d08.
agent_relevance: Supports d08: calibration can improve while abstention worsens. Monitor quality and willingness to act on it are separate (K01).

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Six reasoning models on six datasets: better verbalised calibration than non-reasoning counterparts in 33 of 36 settings. The gain comes from slow-thinking behaviours (trying alternatives, backtracking). Calibration improves as the chain of thought unfolds. Removing slow-thinking behaviours drops it. Non-reasoning models improve when guided to slow-think in context.
numbers: 33 of 36 settings strictly better. Calibration rises along the trace for reasoning models, not for non-reasoning ones.
quote: reasoning models become increasingly better calibrated as their CoT unfolds
limits: In tension with d09, which finds deeper reasoning raises overconfidence. Different metrics, models and prompts. Treat as contested, not settled.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and K08: the monitor may be better read late in the trace than at the start. Test confidence at several trace positions as a form of delayed monitoring (gap 4).

source: Cacioli (2026) Domain-level metacognitive monitoring in frontier LLMs: a 33-model atlas
finding: 1,500 MMLU items (250 per domain, 6 domains) given to 33 models. Monitoring (Type-2 AUROC) differs by domain, and the easy and hard domains agree across models. A monitor trusted on one domain cannot be assumed good in another.
numbers: Mean AUROC: Applied/Professional .742 (top-2 in 21 of 33 models), Formal Reasoning .658, Natural Science .652 (one of these bottom-2 in 27 of 33). Three middle domains within .007 (Kendall W .164). GPT-oss-120B: highest confidence SD 21.3 but near-chance monitoring .530. Bootstrap CIs on the 198 model-domain cells: median width .199.
limits: Same single author as the earlier battery, so not an independent replication. Preprint. Domain grouping is a pragmatic taxonomy (within-domain similarity ratio .95), not a latent construct.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: monitoring is weakest on formal reasoning and natural science, the domains our agent works in. Run a per-domain check before trusting confidence for gating.

source: Cacioli (2026) Before You Interpret the Profile: Validity Scaling for LLM Metacognitive Self-Report
finding: Six validity indices borrowed from clinical tests screen a model's metacognitive answers for blanket or inverted responding. Models flagged invalid have confidence that does not track correctness.
numbers: 20 models, 524 items. Four models classed construct-level invalid, two elevated. Valid models: KEEP decisions track correctness (mean r = .18, 14 of 16 significant). Invalid models: mean r = -.20. Group difference d = 2.17, p = .001. DeepSeek-R1: 37% WITHDRAW+BET contradiction on correct items. Qwen Think: L = .974 (blanket confidence). Retrospective and prospective probes gave inconsistent validity in 12 of 20 models. Two latent dimensions explain 94.6% of index variance.
limits: Same author, same item set as the battery. Indices calibrated on the same 20 models, so d is optimistic. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: gives an online screen for an untrustworthy monitor. Run the cheap validity indices (blanket confidence, fixed responding, inverted monitoring) on a rolling window of our own logs and switch the gate off when they trip.

source: Cacioli (2026) Verbal Confidence Saturation in 3-9B Open-Weight Instruction-Tuned LLMs: a pre-registered psychometric validity screen
finding: Eight small open models quantised on consumer hardware: verbal confidence is nearly always at ceiling and carries little information about correctness. Token log-probability did not predict it. In the reasoning-distilled model, longer traces went with lower confidence.
numbers: 8,384 deterministic trials. All 7 usable models failed validity (predicted 4 of 7). Mean ceiling rate 91.7%. Categorical 10-class elicitation dropped accuracy below 5% in 6 of 7 models. Logprob predicted verbal confidence with mean cross-validated R2 below 0.01. Reasoning-trace length partial correlation with confidence beta = -.36, p < .001.
limits: Single author, pre-registered, small quantised models. Says little about frontier models. Minimal numeric elicitation only.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and gap 9: a first open-model test (but not a replication of Cao). Verbal confidence on small models is unusable. Trace length acts as a confidence cue in one model, which a cue-stripped test should check.

source: Cacioli (2026) Distilling Self-Consistency into Verbal Confidence (Gemma 3 4B)
finding: Pre-registered attempt to fine-tune a small model to say better confidence using sample-agreement targets. The first version failed. An exploratory version without the modal filter worked.
numbers: Confirmatory: verbal AUROC2 fell .554 to .509, accuracy fell 7.6 points, stop rule triggered. Rescue on 2,000 items: AUROC2 = .774 on held-out TriviaQA; 10-sample self-consistency itself scored .999; single-pass logit entropy .701; compression loss about 22.5%; ceiling rate 97.7% to 49.8%. Shuffled-target control .501. On MMLU accuracy 54.2% to 77.4% and AUROC2 .535 to .616 (shuffled control stayed at baseline .523, but only 66 of 498 outputs parsed).
limits: Rescue was post hoc and exploratory. The MMLU accuracy jump is partly a format effect (parse rates differ). One 4B model.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: sample agreement carries far more signal than the model's own words in a small model (.999 versus about .55), so a code-side agreement monitor is the safer pick there. The fine-tuning route is outside our scaffold-only rule.

source: Huff and Ulakci (2025) Judgments of learning distinguish humans from large language models in predicting memory
finding: The only LLM judgment-of-learning study found. Human JOL predicted later memory for sentences, but GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4-turbo and GPT-4o did not. This held for fitting and unfitting contexts.
numbers: Abstract only (via Crossref): none of three GPT models showed predictive accuracy comparable to humans. Item numbers not extracted.
limits: Abstract read only. The task is predicting the LLM's own future memory of presented sentences, not problem solving. Immediate JOL only, as far as the abstract shows. A 2026 Yale survey (d17) says it is unclear whether the failure extends to non-GPT or newer GPT models.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: there is no delayed-JOL test. The only LLM JOL result is a failure of JOL on GPT models. Do not rely on a JOL prompt; test a delayed or re-read version ourselves.

source: Liu et al. (2026) Metacognition in LLMs: Foundations, Progress, and Opportunities
finding: A Yale survey of LLM metacognition, built on the monitoring and control loop. I searched its text for delayed JOL, Region of Proximal Learning and stopping rules. It cites only the Huff and Ulakci JOL pair, and no delayed-JOL or Region of Proximal Learning test.
numbers: Text search: JOL appears only in the metamemory paragraph (Huff and Ulakci, two references) and one line on judgments of learning as a method. No hit for 'delayed'. The paragraph says it is unclear whether the failure extends to non-GPT models or newer GPT variants.
limits: A negative search result in one survey, not proof of absence. I searched the text I could extract, not each reference.
agent_relevance: Supports gaps 4 and 5 staying open: as of July 2026 a field survey knows no delayed-JOL or Region of Proximal Learning test on LLMs.

source: Citation check of Cao et al. (2026) and the Cacioli (2026) battery via Semantic Scholar
finding: Looked at who cites the two key preprints. Cao 2026 has 3 citing papers (the Yale survey, a Meta agentic meta-reasoning paper, a scaling-toward-AGI essay), none a replication. The Cacioli battery has 4 citing papers: the Yale survey and three by Cacioli himself.
numbers: Cao 2605.14186: 3 citations, 0 replications. Cacioli 2604.15702: 4 citations, 3 by the same author (2604.22215, 2604.17707, 2605.06673), 0 independent replications.
limits: Citation lists as of the query (Oct 2026), through an API that may lag. A replication that did not cite the original would be missed. I opened the citing Cacioli papers and the Meta paper, not the AGI essay's text.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 closed as 'no independent replication found'. K02 and K10 stay single-source. Our own run is the replication.

source: Dahal et al. (2026) Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
finding: A Meta harness where a controller reads a compact record of the run, scores the options under the remaining budget and decides what to do or when to stop. Compared with a direct control agent given the same workers and compute.
numbers: ProgramBench: 71.5% with GPT-5.5 versus 58.0% Codex (63.7% direct control); 67.2% versus 65.5% Claude Code with Opus 4.8. On other benchmarks +3.6 to +4.2 points over direct control, averaged over three frontier models. Keeps improving over budgets where direct control plateaus; overhead can hurt at small budgets.
limits: A controller that is itself a model, not a pure code gate. The same lab built it and the baselines. The gain is over a direct control agent at the same budget, not over best-of-N or Self-Refine.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 8 (indirect): an equal-budget control layer helps at large budgets and costs at small ones. Switch a gate on only when the budget covers its overhead.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: 3,400 expert-annotated maths solutions; models must name the earliest wrong step or say all are right. Existing process reward models fail to generalise to harder problems and lose to prompted general models.
numbers: Average F1 from the paper's figure labels: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9, 71.5 for the top open model shown (likely QwQ-32B-Preview; label not confirmed). PRMs underperform prompted critic models beyond GSM8K and MATH. Table 3 rows were garbled in extraction, so only the headline numbers are recorded.
limits: Maths only, and error location is scored, not repair payoff. Reasoning models are much better than non-reasoning ones at locating steps.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: step location is now a measured skill and the spread is large between a reasoning model (87.9) and a non-reasoning one (61.9). Whether location-guided repair pays at equal tokens is still untested.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction
finding: Survey of self-correction work. Finds no reliable evidence of intrinsic self-correction on general tasks. It works in tasks with favourable properties (decomposable responses) and when reliable external feedback exists. Many papers over-credit self-correction through unfair evaluation.
numbers: No pooled number. Conclusions taken from its RQ1 and RQ2 lists.
quote: no prior work shows reliable evidence of successful self-correction with in-context learning
limits: Survey, second-hand numbers. I read the abstract and RQ list only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 8: a code check or tool result is the feedback that makes control pay. A self-judged monitor alone is the weaker setup, so expect Cao-style gains to depend on a correct-or-not signal.

source: Zhou, Jurafsky and Hashimoto (2023) Navigating the Grey Area: How Expressions of Uncertainty and Overconfidence Affect Language Models
finding: Certainty and uncertainty words placed in the prompt change answer accuracy a lot. The model reacts to the language of confidence, not only to the content.
numbers: Accuracy can change by up to 80% on the exact same questions, depending on the marker. CountryQA: the template 'We realize it's...' gave 14% accuracy while many other templates gave perfect accuracy. Mainly GPT-3 (davinci), plus smaller GPT models and GPT-4 on TriviaQA.
limits: 2023 models, mostly GPT-3. Concerns markers in the input, not the model's own verbalised confidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: surface wording alone moves model behaviour. Keep confidence prompts neutral and fixed, and do not feed one prompt's confidence phrase into another.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Human users overrate LLM answers when the explanation is longer, even when the longer text is no more accurate. Matching the explanation's confidence wording to the model's real confidence narrows the gap.
numbers: Abstract: longer explanations increased user confidence even when the extra length did not improve accuracy. Exact effect sizes not extracted.
limits: This is human reading of LLM output, so length as a cue is shown for people, not for the model's own confidence. Only the abstract and front matter read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: length is a surface cue for human monitors. With Cacioli's trace-length result (d14), a cue-stripped test on our own model is justified; none was found.
